=== Morphological Assessment Form ===
A. Leaf Arrangement & Architecture
    1. Leaf relative position (alternate / opposite / whorled): alternate (leaves attach at successive nodes along the stem, alternating sides; no paired leaves at a single node visible)
    2. Leaf spacing (clustered / distal): distal (leaves are spaced out along the stem, not clustered at the apex or base)
B. Leaf Complexity
    3. Leaf complexity (simple / compound): compound (each leaf has multiple leaflets attached to a central rachis)
    4. Compound leaf type, ONLY if leaf complexity is compound (odd-pinnate / even-pinnate): odd-pinnate (terminal leaflet present at the end of the rachis)
    5. Number of leaflets (integer estimate 2, 4, 8, …): 3 (each compound leaf has three leaflets; two lateral and one terminal)
    6. Leaflet arrangement (opposite / alternate / subopposite): subopposite (leaflets appear nearly opposite each other on the rachis, but not perfectly aligned; slight offset visible)
C. Leaf Morphology
    7. Leaf margin (entire / toothed) AND if toothed (dentate, serrate, etc.)): entire (smooth margin without teeth or lobes)
    8. Leaf shape (elliptic, obovate, lanceolate, etc.): elliptic (broadest near the middle, tapering to both ends)
    9. Leaf apex (acute, obtuse, acuminate): acute (tapering to a sharp point)
    10. Leaf base (rounded, cordate, cuneate): cuneate (tapering to a narrow base, wedge-shaped)
    11. Venation type (pinnate / palmate / parallel): pinnate (main vein runs lengthwise, with secondary veins branching off and curving toward the margin)
    12. Secondary veins (visibility, spacing, number): visible, closely spaced, numerous (secondary veins are clearly visible, running from midrib to margin, forming a dense network)
    13. Leaf surface features (glabrous, shiny, dull, rugose): shiny (surface reflects light, indicating a waxy or smooth cuticle)
    14. Leaf surface trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs or fuzz on leaf surface)
    15. Petiole length (short / long): short (petiole is relatively short compared to leaflet length)
    16. Petiole features (winged / grooved / terete): terete (round in cross-section, without wings or grooves)
D. Stem & Shoot Traits
    17. Stem type, may not be visible (woody / herbaceous): herbaceous (stem appears green, flexible, and non-woody)
    18. Stem trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs on stem)
    19. Stem color: green (stem is uniformly green, matching leaf color)
    20. Stem texture (smooth / ridged / lenticellate): smooth (no ridges or lenticels visible; surface is uniform)
E. Other Visible Seedling Traits
    21. Stipules, sometimes visible only in close-up images (present / absent): absent (no stipules observed at leaf bases)
    22. Latex, rarely visible but extremely diagnostic when present (present / not observed): not observed (no latex exudate visible when stem or leaf is broken)
    23. Pulvinus, for Fabaceae family only (present / absent): absent (no swollen joint at leaflet base visible)
    24. Tendrils (present / absent): absent (no tendrils observed)
F. Notes: Some leaves exhibit small circular holes, likely due to mechanical damage or herbivory, but cause not confirmed. White speckling on leaf surface may be mineral deposits or fungal growth, but not clearly identifiable. Pink tag is an artificial marker, not part of the plant. Multiple images confirm consistent morphology across views.

rag_matches.description: Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets apparently never dimorphic, usually 5-9 (rarely 3 or 10), usually alternate, ± elliptic, acuminate, obtuse-attenuate at base, 4-21 cm long, 1.5-8 cm wide, usually glabrous or minutely puberulent and/or strigose on midrib on both surfaces, rarely strigose below; midrib sharply raised. Panicles axillary (often appearing terminal), mostly 8-20 cm long; flowers white or greenish-yellow, 4-6-parted, as wide as long, globular in bud, the trichomes (at least on calyx) erect or appressed; calyx saucer-shaped, the lobes acute or blunt; petals valvate, ovate, to ca 2 mm long, glabrous or sparsely appressed-pubescent outside, glabrous inside, the margins papillose-puberulent; staminal tube two-thirds to three-fourths as long as petals, broader than long, glabrous outside and in but sometimes pubescent inside near apex, the lobes narrowly acute; anthers twice as many as petals, very narrowly ovoid, ca 0.5 mm long, alternating with and usually longer than lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, densely appressed-pubescent with white trichomes all over; style usually glabrous. Capsules ellipsoid, 11-18 mm long, orange at maturity, prominently tuberculate, the 3 (4) valves folding back to expose shiny red aril; seeds 1 or 2, smooth, ellipsoid, ca 1 cm long. Abundant as seedlings; common as adults in the forest, especially in the old forest. Flowering is bimodal, but principally from April to June, especially in June; a second but much smaller flowering period may occur from September to November. [unclear reference] The fruits from the first flowering mature mostly during September and October, especially in October; mature fruits from the second flowering have been seen in June.

Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Life Form: Tree, Shrub 10. Maquira Aubl. By C.C. Berg. Trees or shrubs, dioecious. Leaves alternate, distichous on lateral branches; blade leathery, margins entire, pinnate-veined; stipules not completely amplexicaul, free. Inflorescences on spurs in the axils of the leaves, unisexual, discoid-capitate, involucrate. Staminate inflorescences often several together, pedunculate; flowers not covered by the inner involucral bracts before anthesis, numerous; perianth 4-parted to 4-divided; stamens 4; pistillode absent. Pistillate inflorescences subsessile; flowers numerous; perianth 4-lobed; ovary adnate to the perianth; stigmas 2, tongue-shaped. Fruit-bearing perianth enlarged, fleshy, orange; fruits adnate to the perianth; seed large, without endosperm, cotyledons thick and equal. 4 spp. Tropical America.

Trees, climbing shrubs, or lianas; stipules absent. Leaves compound, odd-pinnate or trifoliate, indumentum of simple trichomes, the blade sometimes with glandular dots on the underside, margin entire; petiole and petiolules pulvinated. Inflorescences in panicles, racemes, or spike-like, axillary or terminal. Flowers bisexual, white, yellowish, or pale pink; sepals 5, valvate or imbricate; petals 5, free; stamens 10, forming a short tube at the base; ovary superior, carpels 1-5, style one per carpel; ovules 2 per carpel. Fruit in follicles, often red; seeds 1 per fruit, black, the aril bright red, yellow, white, or orange.
The family consists of 16 genera and about 300–350 species, pantropical, with a distribution center in western Africa; for tropical America, 5 genera and 108 species are known; 3 genera and 9 species in CR.
It is characterized by its compound leaves, mainly trifoliate or odd-pinnate, leaflets alternate on the rachis, sometimes with dendritic trichomes, petioles clearly pulvinated, stipules absent, and the fruit follicles with a black seed with a reddish basal aril. In vegetative form, its general appearance relates it directly to the family Fabaceae, but several of the characteristics mentioned earlier allow it to be separated.
Traditionally, the family has been placed within the Order Rosales, or in close relation to the Order Sapindales, and some have suggested a link between such Orders. However, recent molecular studies suggest that its placement is in the Order Oxalidales, along with families such as: Oxalidaceae, Cunnoniaceae, Elaeocarpaceae, etc.

Tree, ca. 5-30(-40) m. Leaves imparipinnate, 10-30 cm; petiole and rachis generally canaliculate, glabrous or sparsely puberulent; leaflets 5-9, alternate (rarely subopposite), 10-15(-20) X 2.5-4.5 cm, narrowly elliptical or oblong to oblanceolate, attenuated at the base, acute to acuminate at the apex, subcoriaceous, generally glabrous, with 13-16 secondary veins per side. Inflorescences axillary, thyrsoid, 10-20 cm, glabrous or puberulent. Flowers with petals white to yellowish-green. Fruits yellow to orange, 1.4-2 X 0.8-1.2 cm, oblong to ellipsoid, densely verrucous (with prominent warts often connected by irregular stripes), often sparsely adpressed-pubescent, with 3 or 4 valves; seeds 1 or 2, black, 0.8-2.2 cm, the aril red. Very humid forest, 0-350 m; Pacific slope, [in the Parque Nacional Carara], [in the Puriscal region (in the Parque Nacional La Cangreja)], [in the Parque Nacional Manuel Antonio], [in Uvita], [in the Gulf Dulce region]. Fl. Feb.-Apr., Jun., Dec. [in Costa Rica and Panama], [in Ecuador and Peru], [in Northeast Brazil].

Trees, shrubs, or lianas; twigs often angled or triangularly compound in lianas, ribbed, with simple hair indumentum or rarely with spines; white sap sometimes in lianas (Serjania); stipules often present in lianas (Paullinia, Serjania), absent in tree species; tendrils (modified inflorescence) present in climbing species. Leaves compound (paripinnate, imparipinnate, trifoliate, bipinnate, bi-tri-ternate, etc.), rarely simple (Dodonaea, Llagunoa), alternate, rarely opposite or subopposite (Matayba); rachis often winged, generally with the terminal leaflet aborted in tree species, leaflets normally alternate on the rachis and with entire or serrated margins; petioles pulvinated. Inflorescences terminal, axillary, or sometimes cauliflorous, are panicles, racemes, or fascicles. Flowers generally unisexual; sepals 5-6, free or united; petals 0-5, free, sometimes with a claw; disk present; stamens (5) 8 (10), unequal, pubescent or papillose; carpels 2-3, united; ovary superior, 1-4 locular; placentation usually axillary, ovules 1-2 per locule; style 1, stigmas 2-3. Fruits are capsules, with septicidal or loculicidal dehiscence; drupes or berries, sometimes winged; seeds 1-3 per fruit, globose or flattened, sometimes arillate or with sarcotesta in dehiscent fruits.
The family consists of about 147 genera and 2215 species, mainly pantropical, with only a few genera more diverse in temperate regions, the greatest diversity is concentrated in the Neotropics and the tropics of Asia; the most diverse genera are the lianas Serjania and Paullinia; 21 genera and 90 species in CR; 7 genera and 20 species in LS.
It is recognized by its mainly compound, alternate leaves, the leaflets alternate on the rachis, with margins usually serrated and pulvinated petioles. In tree species, it is common to find at the apex of the rachis the presence of an aborted leaflet; moreover, this group lacks stipules. Stipules are present only in genera of lianas (Paullinia, Serjania, etc.). This is the only family of lianas with compound leaves, with serrated margins and milky sap. The fruits, in general, capsules with (2) 3 parts, with arillate seeds; sometimes indehiscent or drupe-like (Talisia, Sapindus), or winged and the carpels separated into 3 samaras with one seed each (Serjania, Thinouia, Dodonaea).
This family is located in the Order Sapindales, alongside families such as Meliaceae, Rutaceae, Anacardiaceae, etc. The identity of this Order is validated by recent molecular studies, which even suggest that some families considered distinct, e.g., Aceraceae, Hippocastanaceae, etc.; could be reassigned and become part of the family Sapindaceae.
Some fruit trees are directly related to the family, these include: mamón (Melicoccus), rambutan (Nephelium), akí (Bligia), etc. The fruits of Sapindus saponaria (chumino, jaboncillo) have been used as a substitute for soap. Several tree species produce good quality wood. The popular Brazilian drink called guaraná is extracted from Paullinia cupana, which is said to be the plant with the highest caffeine content (Beck, 2004).

Ca. 52 genera and 2850 species, S Can.-Chile and Ven., Trin. & Tob., Guayanas, Bras., Par., Uru., Arg., Antilles, Bahamas, tropical and subtropical of the Old World; 18 genera and 146 species in Costa Rica. Shrubs or trees, rarely suffrutices or (Cassytha) parasitic herbs, hermaphroditic or (less frequently) polygamous, monoecious or dioecious, glabrous or (less frequently) pubescent, with sap generally watery, the foliage usually aromatic, sometimes nauseating (e.g., Cinnamomum sp. 1); stipules absent. Leaves simple, alternate and spiral or (less common) opposite or subopposite (Beilschmiedia, Caryodaphnopsis), entire, usually petiolate. Inflorescence axillary or pseudoterminal, paniculate or (less frequently) racemose, cymose or umbellate, rarely spicate, capitate or with 1 solitary flower. Flowers are bisexual or (sometimes) functionally unisexual, actinomorphic, white to yellowish or green, rarely pink or red, ± small, with a well-developed hypanthium (receptacle) (which looks like a calyx tube), usually persistent and accrescent in fruit, the pedicel sometimes thickened in fruit; members of the perianth (tepals) 6 (in Costa Rica), in 2 whorls of 3 each; stamens functional (3)6-9(12), with or without filament, generally arranged in 3(4) whorls, the 2 outer whorls (which usually appear as one) are absent (rarely) or composed of 6 separate stamens, very similar to each other, the middle whorl is composed of 3 separate stamens (often connivent or connate in Licaria), generally with 2 glands on both sides of each, the inner whorl is absent or composed of 3 staminodes; anthers dehiscent by (1)2-4 valves that open from the base to the apex, usually introrse in the outer whorls (apical-extrorse in Povedadaphne, lateral-extrorse in Pleurothyrium), usually extrorse in the middle whorl; pistil 1, simple; ovary superior (in Costa Rica), unilocular; ovule 1; placentation apical or subapical; style 1; stigma capitate or discoid. Fruit is berry-like or drupe-like, usually green or blackish and held until wrapped by the expanded hypanthium (cup), sometimes reddish, discoid to patelliform (like a plate or cup) or hemispheric to nearly globose, thin to fleshy or woody, smooth to warty or ribbed; seed 1, without endosperm.

Locating an individual
Central Road (CC) 1300 m, Left.
Distribution
From Honduras to Bolivia, Paraguay, and southeastern Brazil. In Costa Rica, widespread in mainly very humid climates on both slopes, 10-1,300 m.
Habit
Tree, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown bark, slightly scaly, inner color pink and with slight resinous-milky secretion, short branches; glabrous twigs; stipules absent.
Bark
Reddish-brown bark, slightly scaly, inner color pink and with slight resinous-milky secretion.
Leaves
Compound odd-pinnate leaves, alternate, leaflets 5-13, 7.5-23 x 2.5-11.2 cm, elliptical to oblong-elliptical, apex short-acuminate, base asymmetric, opposite, glabrous or slightly pubescent on the underside near the central vein, margin entire; petiole 4-20 cm long.
Flowers
Flowers (unisexual) white to yellowish-green and cream; sepals 5, 0.4-0.9 mm long; petals 5, 1.4-2.2 mm long; stamens (8-) 10, unequal, staminodes present in pistillate flowers. The inflorescences have a broad subterminal panicle, with many flowers, 10-35 cm long, rusty-puberulent.
Fruits
Fruit a drupe, 1-1.8 x 0.8-1.3 cm, ovoid, oblong or obovoid, exocarp dark purple to black, endocarp cartilaginous.
Seeds
Seed 1.
Diagnosis
Characterized by its compound leaves, leaflets with entire margins, asymmetric at the base and secondary veins weakly forming a submarginal vein (brochidodromous venation), young leaves with silky pubescence on the underside. Its vegetative appearance and trunk color, as well as its inner bark, resemble or may confuse it with a species of Trichilia (Meliaceae), hence its vernacular names. In mature trees, when making a cut on the trunk, it secretes a slight milky sap in the cambium area.
Habitat
In the rainforest, both in primary forest and secondary vegetation.
Phenology
Flowers observed in May, fruits in October.
